title: Asking a database in plain English
hook: Fixed queries, text-to-SQL on safe views, semantic layers, and why full access is dangerous.
inPlainWords: Text-to-SQL lets a model turn a question like "how many refunds last week?" into a database query. It is powerful, and it needs strong limits, because a model that can write any query can also read or change things it should not.

useCase.title: Let managers ask "which products had the most returns last month?"
useCase.story: Managers want answers from the orders database without waiting for an analyst. The same database holds customer personal data and payment records that most managers must never see.

approaches.name: Pre-written queries behind tools
approaches.what: Developers write and test a fixed set of queries. The model chooses which one and fills in the inputs.
approaches.greatWhen: A known set of common questions.
approaches.avoidWhen: Questions you did not plan for.

approaches.name: Text-to-SQL on safe views
approaches.what: The model writes a query, but only against approved read-only views, with row and column limits.
approaches.example: Query a returns_summary view that has no personal data.

approaches.name: A semantic layer
approaches.what: Define business terms once, like revenue and return rate, so the model uses the agreed meaning.
approaches.example: "Return rate" always means returned units divided by shipped units.

approaches.name: Human-checked queries
approaches.what: Show the generated query and result to an analyst before it is trusted.
approaches.example: An analyst approves a finance query.

approaches.name: Full database access for the model
approaches.what: The model can run any query on the live database.
approaches.avoidWhen: Anything real. It risks data leaks, costly queries and damage.
approaches.example: A model runs a delete, or exports every customer email.

challenge.question: Managers want flexible answers, but the database holds personal and payment data. What is the safest useful design?

options.text: Text-to-SQL limited to read-only approved views, with a semantic layer, row and time limits, and query logs
options.why: Flexible for managers, and the database itself enforces the limits.

options.text: Give the model admin access so it can answer anything
options.why: One clever question could leak or destroy data.

options.text: Only pre-written queries, with no flexibility
options.why: Very safe, but managers keep asking analysts for anything new.

options.text: Let the model guess table names from memory
options.why: It will invent tables and get wrong numbers.

bestCase.title: Flexible questions, on safe views, with logged queries
bestCase.example: "Which products had the most returns last month?" The model writes a query against the returns_summary view. The semantic layer defines return rate, the database enforces read-only access with a time limit, and the query and answer are logged. The manager also sees the query used.

worstCase.title: A model with the keys to the whole database
worstCase.example: A manager asks to "export everything about our best customers". The model runs a query that returns names, emails and card tokens. Another vague question triggers a huge query that slows the live store.

route.travelling: "Which products had the most returns last month?"

steps.label: Model reads the approved schema
steps.goes: It sees only the safe views and their business definitions.
steps.goesWrong: It sees every table, including personal and payment data.

steps.label: Model writes a query
steps.goes: It writes a query against returns_summary.

steps.label: Safety checks
steps.goes: Read-only, limited rows and time, no personal columns.

steps.label: Run on a read copy
steps.goes: The query runs on a copy so the live store is not slowed.

steps.label: Answer, with the query shown
steps.goes: The manager sees the result and the query. Everything is logged.

takeaway: Let the model write questions, not commands. Give it approved read-only views, agreed definitions, and logs.
